headline: Rhode Island audit finds gaps in opioid treatment records and $875,696 in potential Medicaid overpayments
dek: A review of 100 sampled medication-assisted-treatment claims found every claim missed at least one federal or state requirement, while a separate billing review identified 6,347 potentially improper payments.
body: A Rhode Island performance audit released Wednesday found widespread documentation and service-delivery problems in the state’s opioid treatment programs, with every one of 100 sampled medication-assisted-treatment claims failing at least one federal or state requirement. The same review identified $875,696 in potential Medicaid overpayments tied to daily methadone billing that should have been submitted as weekly bundled claims.

The [Rhode Island Office of the Auditor General report](https://www.oag.ri.gov/reports-performance/OpioidProviderCompliance-20261003.pdf), prepared with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, examined the state’s oversight of opioid treatment services from Jan. 1, 2023, through Dec. 31, 2024. Five providers submitted claims for 274,412 medication-assisted-treatment services totaling $25.54 million during that period. Auditors selected 100 services for detailed testing; the sample was designed to evaluate compliance, not to establish that every service delivered statewide was deficient.

The problems covered core parts of treatment. Auditors recorded 99 instances in which the sampled claims did not satisfy medication-assisted-treatment requirements, 95 problems with intake or five-year biopsychosocial assessments, 75 missing or incomplete six-month treatment-plan reviews and 70 failures involving required counseling sessions. They also found deficiencies in annual assessments, treatment plans, medical examinations and toxicology screening. The audit said 22 of the 100 client cases did not meet the minimum annual toxicology-testing requirement, and seven had no toxicology tests documented.

The report describes opioid treatment programs as federally certified and state-licensed providers that dispense methadone and other medications while also providing counseling, medical evaluation and recovery support. Rhode Island rules require patients in maintenance treatment to receive random toxicology testing at least eight times per year, annual medical examinations and documented treatment planning. Those records are not merely administrative paperwork: the auditor said missing examinations, counseling notes or safety instructions can make it harder to identify medical problems, monitor relapse risks, coordinate care and manage medication safely.

The audit also estimated that 274,412 medication-assisted-treatment services during the review period, totaling $24.92 million, did not meet enough documented requirements to support Medicaid reimbursement. That estimate is different from the $875,696 figure, which concerns a specific billing problem. Auditors and federal investigators validated 6,347 claims in which providers billed daily methadone encounters instead of the required single weekly bundled claim. In some cases, providers submitted five to seven daily claims for one beneficiary in the same week, causing Medicaid to pay more than the established bundled rate. The report calls the amount potential overpayments, not a final fraud finding.

Rhode Island’s Executive Office of Health and Human Services said a full investigation and data analysis of the relevant billing code had been completed and that corrective-action plans involving recoupments were under review. The agency also said it was reassessing its Medicaid system configuration with Gainwell Technologies, updating billing guidance and planning quarterly surveillance of the code. The audit recommends reviewing all adjudicated and pending claims, recovering amounts determined to be improper and returning the federal share.

The state behavioral-health department outlined a separate response to the clinical-documentation findings. It plans to keep biennial audits but add six-month post-audit reviews, routine unannounced visits and standardized documentation samples from all five providers. The department also said providers will conduct internal audits at least every six months, receive mandatory training and eventually be measured through a centralized compliance dashboard. Providers that remain below a compliance threshold or show recurring deficiencies may be required to submit correction plans and face licensing or administrative action.

Providence Business News independently reported the audit’s finding of 100 out of 100 sampled claims with compliance failures and the potential overpayment total. The report’s release comes after a separate June settlement in which Journey to Hope Health and Healing and its former chief executive agreed to pay $10.2 million to resolve federal and state allegations involving treatment services and Medicaid claims; the Justice Department said that case concerned conduct from 2015 through 2021 and is not the same matter as the new audit. The next measurable test for Rhode Island will be whether the promised claims review, billing controls and provider monitoring produce recoveries and better documentation without disrupting access to treatment.

The audit does not identify the individual patients whose records were sampled, and its findings do not mean every Rhode Island treatment provider or every patient encounter failed. They do show that the state’s existing oversight did not provide the assurance auditors expected across the sampled claims. For patients and families, the practical issue is whether the corrective steps improve continuity and safety in programs that play a central role in treating opioid-use disorder. For taxpayers, the open questions are how much of the potential overpayment is confirmed, how much is recovered and whether new system edits prevent the same billing pattern from recurring.
location: Rhode Island Office of the Auditor General, Providence, Rhode Island
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Rhode Island audit flags opioid-treatment Medicaid overpayments
seoDescription: A Rhode Island audit found every one of 100 sampled opioid-treatment Medicaid claims had a compliance failure and identified $875,696 in potential overpayments.
